claim: The structure of supercomplex I1III2IV1 from bovine heart mitochondria was determined by cryo-EM at 9 Å resolution.
source: We determined the structure of supercomplex I1III2IV1 from bovine heart mitochondria by cryo-EM at 9 Å resolution.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the resolution achieved for the structure determination.

claim: Most protein-protein contacts between complex I, III and IV in the membrane are mediated by supernumerary subunits.
source: Most protein-protein contacts between complex I, III and IV in the membrane are mediated by supernumerary subunits.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis shown in the results.

claim: One of the two Rieske iron-sulfur cluster domains in the complex III dimer is resolved, indicating that this domain is immobile and unable to transfer electrons.
source: Of the two Rieske iron-sulfur cluster domains in the complex III dimer, one is resolved, indicating that this domain is immobile and unable to transfer electrons.
evidence: The abstract states this observation and provides interpretation based on structural data.

claim: The diffusion distance between the active complex III monomer and complex I is 11 nm.
source: The central position of the active complex III monomer between complex I and IV in the respirasome is optimal for accepting reduced quinone from complex I over a short diffusion distance of 11 nm, and delivering reduced cytochrome c to complex IV.
evidence: The abstract provides a specific measurement of the diffusion distance.

claim: The functional asymmetry of complex III provides strong evidence for directed electron flow from complex I to complex IV through the active complex III monomer in the mammalian supercomplex.
source: The functional asymmetry of complex III provides strong evidence for directed electron flow from complex I to complex IV through the active complex III monomer in the mammalian supercomplex.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract based on the structural findings.

claim: Mammalian complex I comprises 44 different subunits, including two copies of subunit SDAP, and therefore consists of a total of 45 subunits.
source: Mammalian complex I comprises 44 different subunits, including two copies of subunit SDAP, and therefore consists of a total of 45 subunits (Vinothkumar et al., 2014).
evidence: This compositional information is cited from a previous study.

claim: The 14 core subunits of complex I are conserved from prokaryotes to mammals.
source: The 14 core subunits are conserved from prokaryotes to mammals (Walker, 1992).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the conservation claim.

claim: Complex I pumps four protons from the matrix to the cristae lumen per catalytic cycle.
source: As a third unit, the membrane-embedded transporter assembly pumps four protons from the matrix to the cristae lumen per catalytic cycle (Galkin and Terenetskaya, 1999; Leif et al., 1995).
evidence: This functional property is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Complex II is the only complex in the electron transfer chain that does not translocate protons.
source: Succinate:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, or complex II, is the only complex in the electron transfer chain that does not translocate protons, but merely feeds electrons into the process.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing characteristic of complex II.

claim: The cytochrome bc1 complex (complex III) is a symmetrical dimer.
source: The cytochrome bc1 complex (complex III) is a symmetrical dimer, with cytochrome b, the Rieske iron-sulfur protein and cytochrome c1 as core subunits (Yang and Trumpower, 1986).
evidence: This structural property is stated with a citation.

claim: In mammals, complex III contains a total of 11 subunits per monomer, of which eight are supernumerary.
source: In mammals, complex III contains a total of 11 subunits per monomer, of which eight are supernumerary (Schägger et al., 1986).
evidence: This compositional information is cited from a previous study.

claim: Mammalian complex IV has three core subunits (COX1, COX2 and COX3) and 14 subunits in total.
source: Mammalian complex IV has three core subunits (COX1, COX2 and COX3) and 14 subunits in total (Balsa et al., 2012; Kadenbach et al., 1983).
evidence: This compositional information is cited from previous studies.

claim: The discovery of supercomplexes by blue-native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (BN-PAGE) after solubilization with mild detergents gave rise to the plasticity model.
source: The discovery of supercomplexes by blue-native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (BN-PAGE) after solubilization with mild detergents (Schägger and Pfeiffer, 2000) gave rise to the plasticity model, which postulates that respiratory complexes can exist both free in the membrane and as larger supramolecular entities (Acin-Perez et al., 2008; D'Aurelio et al., 2006).
evidence: This historical development is stated with citations.

claim: The respirasome (supercomplex I1III2IV1) contains all components required to transfer electrons from NADH to molecular oxygen.
source: The respirasome contains all components required to transfer electrons from NADH to molecular oxygen (Schägger and Pfeiffer, 2000).
evidence: This functional property is stated with a citation.

claim: Advantages due to partitioning of the quinol pool and substrate channeling have been postulated and are supported by several independent studies.
source: At the functional level, advantages due to partitioning of the quinol pool and substrate channeling have been postulated and are supported by several independent studies (Bianchi et al., 2003; Lapuente-Brun et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Other results are inconsistent with a partitioning of the quinol pool.
source: Other results are inconsistent with a partitioning of the quinol pool (Blaza et al., 2014).
evidence: This contradictory finding is cited from another study.

claim: A reduction in the level of reactive oxygen species (ROS) has been suggested as a possible role for supercomplexes.
source: A reduction in the level of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that are generated as side products of electron transfer reactions in the respiratory chain has also been suggested as a possible role (Maranzana et al., 2013; Panov et al., 2006; Seelert et al., 2009).
evidence: This proposed function is cited from multiple studies.

claim: Supercomplexes have been proposed to confer stability to complex I or assist in its assembly.
source: From the point of view of protein structure, supercomplexes have been proposed to confer stability to complex I or assist in its assembly (Marques et al., 2007; Schägger et al., 2004).
evidence: This proposed structural role is cited from previous studies.

claim: Recent complexome profiling studies failed to detect supercomplexes containing immature complex I, suggesting that the respirasome forms by association of fully assembled component complexes.
source: However, recent complexome profiling studies failed to detect supercomplexes containing immature complex I, suggesting that the respirasome forms by association of fully assembled component complexes (Guerrero-Castillo et al., 2016).
evidence: This finding is cited from a recent study.

claim: Genetic mutations that impair the assembly of complex III result in a loss of complex I and combined complex III/I defects.
source: Genetic mutations that impair the assembly of complex III result in a loss of complex I and combined complex III/I defects (Acin-Perez et al., 2004; Bruno et al., 2003; Lamantea et al., 2002; Schägger et al., 2004).
evidence: This pathological observation is cited from multiple studies.

claim: Complex IV deficiencies associated with a reduction of complex I levels in mouse and human cells have been reported.
source: Complex IV deficiencies associated with a reduction of complex I levels in mouse and human cells have also been reported (D'Aurelio et al., 2006; Diaz et al., 2006; Vempati et al., 2009).
evidence: This observation is cited from multiple studies.

claim: Low levels of cytochrome bc1 and cytochrome c oxidase result in an accumulation of reduced quinone, which would trigger reverse electron transfer (RET) and generation of superoxide by complex I.
source: Recent studies suggest however that low levels of cytochrome bc1 and cytochrome c oxidase (as well as cytochrome c) result in an accumulation of reduced quinone, which would trigger reverse electron transfer (RET) and generation of superoxide by complex I. This could result in oxidative damage and complex I degradation (Guaras et al., 2016).
evidence: This mechanism is cited from a recent study.

claim: When ROS production by RET was inhibited, complex I levels were restored.
source: When ROS production by RET was inhibited, complex I levels were restored (Guaras et al., 2016).
evidence: This experimental result is cited from a study.

claim: Structures of the isolated respirasome at estimated resolutions of 20–30 Å have been obtained by negative-stain electron microscopy (EM), single-particle cryo-EM and electron cryo-tomography.
source: Structures of the isolated respirasome at estimated resolutions of 20–30 Å have been obtained by negative-stain electron microscopy (EM) (Schäfer et al., 2007), single-particle cryo-EM (Althoff et al., 2011) and electron cryo-tomography (Dudkina et al., 2011).
evidence: Previous structural studies are cited.

claim: Two cryo-EM studies of the respirasome from ovine and porcine heart mitochondria have been published since this manuscript was submitted.
source: Two cryo-EM studies of the respirasome from ovine and porcine heart mitochondria have been published since this manuscript was submitted (Gu et al., 2016; Letts et al., 2016b).
evidence: The authors cite two studies published after their submission.

claim: Both ovine and porcine respirasome studies are at significantly higher resolution than the bovine structure.
source: Both are at significantly higher resolution than our structure, but neither of them observe the functional asymmetry of complex III, which we regard to be the most important functional insight from the respirasome structure.
evidence: The authors compare their work to the two published studies.

claim: Neither the ovine nor porcine respirasome studies observe the functional asymmetry of complex III.
source: Both are at significantly higher resolution than our structure, but neither of them observe the functional asymmetry of complex III, which we regard to be the most important functional insight from the respirasome structure.
evidence: The authors compare their findings to the two published studies.

claim: PCC-a-M solubilizes mitochondria efficiently while preserving the interactions between complexes I, III and IV.
source: In an initial screen, we identified a narrow concentration range in which PCC-a-M solubilizes mitochondria efficiently, while preserving the interactions between complexes I, III and IV (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Supercomplex I1III2IV1 purified from membranes solubilized with PCC-a-M was pure, whereas with digitonin, 42% of the particles had lost complex IV.
source: Image analysis of negatively stained samples confirmed that supercomplex I1III2IV1 purified from membranes solubilized with PCC-a-M was pure, whereas with digitonin, 42% of the particles had lost complex IV (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by image analysis data shown in the figure supplement.

claim: A total of 156,519 particles was picked manually and classified in RELION 1.4.
source: A total of 156,519 particles was picked manually and classified in RELION 1.4 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the data processing workflow.

claim: The most homogeneous class of 17,094 particles (class 1; 11% of the total) yielded a structure of the respirasome at a final resolution of 9.1 Å.
source: The most homogeneous class of 17,094 particles (class 1; 11% of the total) yielded a structure of the respirasome at a final resolution of 9.1 Å.
evidence: This describes the final resolution achieved for the main structure.

claim: A second structure of supercomplex I1III2IV1 with distinctly different features was resolved to 10.4 Å (class 2; 6% of the total).
source: A second structure of supercomplex I1III2IV1 with distinctly different features was resolved to 10.4 Å (class 2; 6% of the total).
evidence: This describes an alternative conformation observed in the data.

claim: A third class with 12,042 particles lacking complex IV (class 3; 8% of the total) was refined to 9.9 Å.
source: Lastly, a third class with 12,042 particles lacking complex IV (class 3; 8% of the total) was refined to 9.9 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes a subcomplex observed in the data.

claim: At an estimated local resolution of 8.6 Å, the transmembrane region of class 1 indicates clear densities for most of the 132 membrane-spanning α–helices in the supercomplex.
source: At an estimated local resolution of 8.6 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the transmembrane region of class 1 indicates clear densities for most of the 132 membrane-spanning α–helices in the supercomplex (Figure 2B).
evidence: This describes the quality of the density map in the transmembrane region.

claim: Atomic models for bovine complex I, III and IV were docked into the 3D maps with excellent fit.
source: Atomic models for bovine complex I (Vinothkumar et al., 2014), III (Iwata et al., 1998) and IV (Tsukihara et al., 1996) were docked into the 3D maps. The fit was excellent for all three complexes in all map regions.
evidence: This describes the model fitting procedure and quality.

claim: With one exception, all inter-complex contacts involve supernumerary subunits.
source: With one exception, all inter-complex contacts involve supernumerary subunits.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: Subunit B22 of complex I is in touch with subunit 1 of complex III at a minimum distance of 4 Å.
source: In the matrix, subunit B22 of complex I is in touch with subunit 1 of complex III at a minimum distance of 4 Å.
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the structure.

claim: Subunit B14.7 of complex I approaches subunit 8 of cytochrome bc1 near both membrane surfaces to within sidechain contact.
source: In the membrane region, subunit B14.7 of complex I approaches subunit 8 of cytochrome bc1 near both membrane surfaces to within sidechain contact (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a specific structural observation shown in Figure 3.

claim: Subunit B14.7 establishes clear contacts with complex III within the hydrophobic interior of the respirasome.
source: In the centre of the supercomplex, subunit B14.7 establishes clear contacts with complex III within the hydrophobic interior of the respirasome.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the map.

claim: Contacts between complexes I and IV are mediated by subunit ND5 of complex I that approaches complex IV subunit COX7C to within an α–carbon distance of around 10 Å at the membrane surface on the matrix side.
source: Contacts between complexes I and IV are mediated by subunit ND5 of complex I that approaches complex IV subunit COX7C to within an α–carbon distance of around 10 Å at the membrane surface on the matrix side.
evidence: This is a specific measurement from the structure.

claim: ND5 appears to be the only one of the 14 complex I core subunits that is involved directly in supercomplex formation.
source: ND5 appears to be the only one of the 14 complex I core subunits that is involved directly in supercomplex formation.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis.

claim: The interface between complexes III and IV is formed by subunits 1, 9 and 10 of the bc1 complex and COX7A1 of cytochrome c oxidase.
source: The interface between complexes III and IV is formed by subunits 1, 9 and 10 of the bc1 complex and COX7A1 of cytochrome c oxidase.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the map.

claim: Subunit 9 of complex III has previously been shown to be required for stable interaction with cytochrome c oxidase.
source: Subunit 9 of complex III has previously been shown to be required for stable interaction with cytochrome c oxidase (Zara et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: Classes 1 and 2 are related by a 25° rigid-body rotation of the whole complex III dimer relative to complex I, around an axis roughly perpendicular to the membrane plane.
source: Classes 1 and 2 are related by a 25° rigid-body rotation of the whole complex III dimer relative to complex I, around an axis roughly perpendicular to the membrane plane.
evidence: This describes the conformational difference between two classes.

claim: In class 2, the matrix arm of complex I has moved away from the center of the supercomplex by a rotation of 3–4° around an axis parallel to the membrane.
source: In class 2, the matrix arm of complex I has moved away from the center of the supercomplex by a rotation of 3–4° around an axis parallel to the membrane (Figure 4B).
evidence: This describes a conformational change observed in class 2.

claim: Structures of active and deactive states of complex I have been recently presented, which differ by a similar movement of the matrix arm.
source: Structures of active and deactive states of complex I have been recently presented, which differ by a similar movement of the matrix arm (Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a recent study.

claim: Class 2 may represent a subpopulation of the supercomplex in which complex I is in the deactive state.
source: Class 2 may thus represent a subpopulation of the supercomplex in which complex I is in the deactive state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the class 2 structure.

claim: Class 2 may result from rearrangement or destabilization of the supercomplex during purification.
source: Alternatively, class 2 may result from rearrangement or destabilization of the supercomplex during purification.
evidence: This is an alternative speculative interpretation.

claim: The mutual arrangement of complexes I and III in class 3 is the same as in class 1.
source: The mutual arrangement of complexes I and III in class 3 is the same as in class 1, confirming that the interaction between these two proteins is sufficiently stable to fix them in this specific conformation (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the two classes.

claim: Several of the classes obtained (~30% of the initial dataset) have no density for the NADH:dehydrogenase module of complex I, or even lack the whole matrix arm.
source: Several of the classes obtained (~30% of the initial dataset) have no density for the NADH:dehydrogenase module of complex I, or even lack the whole matrix arm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes heterogeneity observed in the dataset.

claim: A recent study of respirasome biogenesis has suggested that supercomplexes form by association of individual subunits of the respiratory complexes or their intermediate assemblies, rather than from the fully assembled respiratory chain complexes.
source: A recent study of respirasome biogenesis (Moreno-Lastres et al., 2012) has suggested that supercomplexes form by association of individual subunits of the respiratory complexes or their intermediate assemblies, rather than from the fully assembled respiratory chain complexes.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The incorporation of the NADH:dehydrogenase module of complex I has been presented as the final step in the assembly process.
source: The incorporation of the NADH:dehydrogenase module of complex I has been presented as the final step in the assembly process (Moreno-Lastres et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The density for the 51 kDa subunit is weak in the 8.1 Å global average.
source: These observations are in agreement with our 8.1 Å global average (Figure 4C,D), in which the density for the 51 kDa subunit is weak and could explain why the NADH:dehydrogenase module is absent in several of the 3D class averages (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the density map.

claim: Several of the nuclear-encoded subunits in the mature enzyme can be exchanged against newly imported copies, in parallel to the de novo assembly of the complex.
source: It has been shown that several of the nuclear-encoded subunits in the mature enzyme can be exchanged against newly imported copies, in parallel to the de novo assembly of the complex (Dieteren et al., 2012; Lazarou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Most subunits of the N-catalytic unit are particularly susceptible to oxidative damage.
source: This holds true for most subunits of the N-catalytic unit (Dieteren et al., 2012; Lazarou et al., 2007), which are particularly susceptible to oxidative damage.
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: A direct replacement of N-catalytic unit subunits would provide an efficient means of repairing oxidative damage of complex I.
source: A direct replacement of these subunits would provide an efficient means of repairing oxidative damage of complex I (Dieteren et al., 2012; Lazarou et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: The iron-sulfur domain is the active part of the Rieske protein subunit of the bc1 complex that carries electrons from the QP site via its iron-sulfur cluster to heme c1.
source: The iron-sulfur domain is the active part of the Rieske protein subunit of the bc1 complex that carries electrons from the QP site via its iron-sulfur cluster to heme c1, where they are picked up by the small, soluble cytochrome c protein for transfer to complex IV (Kühlbrandt, 2015).
evidence: This describes the function of the iron-sulfur domain with a citation.

claim: In order to transfer electrons to c1, the iron-sulfur domain has to move on a hinge by 10–15 Å.
source: In order to transfer electrons to c1, the iron-sulfur domain has to move on a hinge by 10–15 Å (Iwata et al., 1998).
evidence: This is cited from a previous structural study.

claim: When the hinge movement of the iron-sulfur domain is blocked, no electrons are transferred to cytochrome c1.
source: The hinge movement of the iron-sulfur domain is essential for function since when it is blocked, no electrons are transferred to cytochrome c1 (Darrouzet et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The fact that one of the two iron-sulfur domains in the supercomplex is resolved means that one of the two complex III monomers is inactive.
source: The fact that one of the two iron-sulfur domains in the supercomplex is resolved means that one of the two complex III monomers is inactive.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: The inactive monomer is the one in contact with the well-defined iron-sulfur domain.
source: The inactive monomer is the one in contact with the well-defined iron-sulfur domain.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: The active monomer near the disordered iron-sulfur domain is surrounded by complex I, complex IV and the inactive complex III monomer.
source: The active monomer near the disordered iron-sulfur domain is surrounded by complex I, complex IV and the inactive complex III monomer (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a structural observation shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For the bacterial cytochrome bc1 complex, it has been shown that there is no difference in the electron transport activity if one of its monomers is permanently inactivated by mutagenesis.
source: However, for the bacterial cytochrome bc1 complex, which is a simpler version of mitochondrial complex III and likewise dimeric, it has been shown that there is no difference in the electron transport activity of the bc1 complex if one of its monomers is permanently inactivated by mutagenesis (Castellani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study on bacterial complex.

claim: In bacteria only one half of the bc1 dimer is required for electron transfer.
source: Therefore, in bacteria only one half of the bc1 dimer is required for electron transfer, and this most likely holds true for the mitochondrial complex as well.
evidence: This is an inference from the bacterial study applied to mitochondria.

claim: In the bacterial complex, the choice of the active monomer is thought to be random.
source: In the bacterial complex, the choice of the active monomer is thought to be random (Covian and Trumpower, 2008), whereas in the respirasome, the active monomer is clearly the one in the centre of the supercomplex.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study on bacterial complex.

claim: In the respirasome, the active monomer is clearly the one in the centre of the supercomplex.
source: In the bacterial complex, the choice of the active monomer is thought to be random (Covian and Trumpower, 2008), whereas in the respirasome, the active monomer is clearly the one in the centre of the supercomplex.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: Under normal turnover conditions, the two monomers of complex III are not active simultaneously.
source: Under normal turnover conditions, the two monomers of complex III are not active simultaneously (Castellani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: A model for electron transfer within complex III has been proposed, in which the activation of either monomer is random and both monomers switch between active and inactive states.
source: A model for electron transfer within complex III has been proposed, in which the activation of either monomer is random and both monomers switch between active and inactive states (Covian and Trumpower, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: In the various crystal structures of complex III, the iron-sulfur domains occupy different positions, either as a result of crystal contacts or in response to the occupancy of the QP site.
source: In the various crystal structures of complex III, the iron-sulfur domains occupy different positions, either as a result of crystal contacts or, more significantly, in response to the occupancy of the QP site (Berry et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: In single particle cryo-EM conformational changes are not subject to crystal contacts.
source: In single particle cryo-EM conformational changes are not subject to such contacts.
evidence: This is a general principle of cryo-EM methodology.

claim: In the absence of inhibitors, a cryo-EM map of complex III should reveal two equally unresolved iron-sulfur domains, as a result of averaging particles in different states.
source: Therefore, in the absence of inhibitors, and in light of the known mechanism of electron transfer, a cryo-EM map of complex III should reveal two equally unresolved iron-sulfur domains, as a result of averaging particles in different states.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known mechanism and cryo-EM principles.

claim: The observed asymmetry is incompatible with an alternating activation of the two complex III monomers.
source: The observed asymmetry is thus incompatible with an alternating activation of the two complex III monomers and implies that each monomer has a different function.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observation.

claim: In the respirasome, the central monomer of complex III preferentially catalyzes quinol oxidation.
source: Our data suggest that in the respirasome, the central monomer of complex III preferentially catalyzes quinol oxidation.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural analysis.

claim: Electrons can equilibrate rapidly between the two bL hemes.
source: As electrons can equilibrate rapidly between the two bL hemes (Castellani et al., 2010), quinone reduction may occur in either monomer, although it is possible that the distal monomer has no function, except as a scaffold.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: The quinol oxidation site of the active complex III monomer faces the site on complex I where the reduced quinol is released.
source: In the respirasome, the quinol oxidation site of the active complex III monomer faces the site on complex I where the reduced quinol is released.
evidence: This is a structural observation.

claim: The shortest distance between the quinol release site on complex I and the quinol oxidation site of the active complex III monomer is about 11 nm.
source: The shortest distance between the two sites is about 11 nm (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a measurement from the structure shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The quinol oxidation site of the inactive monomer is on the far side of the dimer, at a distance of at least 18 nm from the complex I site.
source: The quinol oxidation site of the inactive monomer is on the far side of the dimer, at a distance of at least 18 nm from the complex I site, assuming that the quinol cannot pass through the complex III dimer.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structure with an assumption.

claim: A quinol diffusing through the lipid bilayer from complex I to complex III would encounter the active monomer first.
source: A quinol diffusing through the lipid bilayer from complex I to complex III would thus encounter the active monomer first.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural arrangement.

claim: Only one of the complex III monomers is well-placed to accept reduced quinol from complex I, which may explain why only this monomer is active.
source: Significantly, only one of the complex III monomers is well-placed to accept reduced quinol from complex I, which may explain why only this monomer is active.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural arrangement.

claim: Results inconsistent with the existence of distinct quinone pools and substrate channeling have been reported.
source: Results inconsistent with the existence of distinct quinone pools and substrate channeling have been reported (Blaza et al., 2014), but substrate channeling between complexes I and III is supported by most studies of metabolic flux control (Bianchi et al., 2003; Lapuente-Brun et al., 2013) and in recent reviews discussing the results of Blaza et al (Enríquez, 2016; Lenaz et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites both contradictory and supporting evidence from the literature.

claim: The asymmetry observed for complex III in the supercomplex structure is in agreement with substrate channeling and provides further support for electron transfer by substrate channeling in the respirasome.
source: The asymmetry observed for complex III in our supercomplex structure is in agreement with these results and provides further support for electron transfer by substrate channeling in the respirasome.
evidence: This is a conclusion connecting the structural findings to the functional debate.

claim: The cytochrome c binding site on the active bc1 monomer is about 10 Å closer to complex IV than that of the inactive monomer.
source: The cytochrome c binding site on the active bc1 monomer is about 10 Å closer to complex IV than that of the inactive monomer.
evidence: This is a measurement from the structure.

claim: Complex IV needs four electrons, and hence four cytochromes c, to produce one molecule of water.
source: Complex IV needs four electrons, and hence four cytochromes c, to produce one molecule of water.
evidence: This is established biochemical knowledge.

claim: The proximity of the binding sites may be an important advantage by minimizing the time for each of the four cytochrome c transfer steps.
source: The proximity of the binding sites, which would minimize the time for each of the four cytochrome c transfer steps, may be an important advantage.
evidence: This is a speculative functional interpretation.

claim: In photosystem II, one of two near-symmetrical electron transfer chains has been turned off in the course of evolution to avoid wasteful electron transfer to two identical quinol electron acceptors.
source: Our observation that in the respirasome only one of two possible electron transfer branches is active is reminiscent of the two near-symmetrical electron transfer chains in photosystem II, one of which has been turned off in the course of evolution to avoid wasteful electron transfer to two identical quinol electron acceptors (Nelson and Yocum, 2006).
evidence: This is cited from a previous study on photosystem II.

claim: Point mutations or truncation of the mitochondrially encoded cytochrome b subunit of complex III cause progressive exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis in human patients.
source: However, point mutations (Bruno et al., 2003) or truncation (Lamantea et al., 2002) of the mitochondrially encoded cytochrome b subunit of complex III that cause progressive exercise intolerance and lactic acidosis in human patients were found to not only reduce the levels of complex III but also that of complex I.
evidence: This is cited from previous clinical studies.

claim: The depletion of complex III levels in the membrane results in a secondary loss of complex I.
source: Biochemical studies of similar mutants established that the depletion of complex III levels in the membrane results in a secondary loss of complex I (Acin-Perez et al., 2004; Schägger et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from previous biochemical studies.

claim: Stable expression of complex I in the absence of complex III has been demonstrated through direct or indirect inhibition of ROS production by RET.
source: More recently, stable expression of complex I in the absence of complex III has been demonstrated through direct or indirect inhibition of ROS production by RET (Guaras et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from a recent study.

claim: Inhibition of cytochrome bc1 activity was insufficient to induce complete degradation of complex I.
source: Inhibition of cytochrome bc1 activity however was insufficient to induce complete degradation of complex I (Acin-Perez et al., 2004; Guaras et al., 2016), suggesting that physical interaction between the complexes has an at least partially stabilizing effect.
evidence: This is cited from previous studies.

claim: Physical interaction between the complexes has an at least partially stabilizing effect on complex I.
source: Inhibition of cytochrome bc1 activity however was insufficient to induce complete degradation of complex I (Acin-Perez et al., 2004; Guaras et al., 2016), suggesting that physical interaction between the complexes has an at least partially stabilizing effect.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited studies.

claim: The nuclear-encoded, supernumerary complex I subunit B14.7 evidently has a major part in the formation and stability of the respirasome.
source: The nuclear-encoded, supernumerary complex I subunit B14.7 (Figure 3) evidently has a major part in the formation and stability of the respirasome.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: A point mutation in subunit B14.7 is associated with complex I deficiency in patients with fatal infantile lactic acidemia.
source: A point mutation in this subunit is associated with complex I deficiency in patients with fatal infantile lactic acidemia (Berger et al., 2008), and a disruption of the gene of the homologous protein in the fungus Neurospora crassa results in incomplete assembly of complex I (Nehls et al., 1992).
evidence: This is cited from previous clinical and genetic studies.

claim: A disruption of the gene of the homologous protein to B14.7 in the fungus Neurospora crassa results in incomplete assembly of complex I.
source: A point mutation in this subunit is associated with complex I deficiency in patients with fatal infantile lactic acidemia (Berger et al., 2008), and a disruption of the gene of the homologous protein in the fungus Neurospora crassa results in incomplete assembly of complex I (Nehls et al., 1992).
evidence: This is cited from a previous genetic study.

claim: The ovine complex I has been described as being particularly stable and suitable for structural studies.
source: The ovine complex I has been described as being particularly stable and suitable for structural studies (Letts et al., 2016a) and the same most likely holds true for supercomplexes.
evidence: This is cited from a previous study.

claim: At resolutions of 5–6 Å, both ovine and porcine structures corroborate most of the protein-protein contacts observed in the bovine complex.
source: At resolutions of 5–6 Å, both structures corroborate most of the protein-protein contacts we observe in the bovine complex.
evidence: This is a comparison with the two published structures.

claim: Several additional subunits were found to participate in the stabilization of the supercomplex in the higher resolution structures, which were not clearly visible at the bovine map resolution.
source: Several additional subunits were found to participate in the stabilization of the supercomplex, which were not clearly visible at our map resolution.
evidence: This is a comparison with the two published structures.

claim: Only one of the two new studies found a second significant respirasome conformation at an overall resolution of 6.7 Å.
source: Of the two new studies, only one (Letts et al., 2016b) found a second significant respirasome conformation at an overall resolution of 6.7 Å.
evidence: This is a comparison with the published studies.

claim: The tight conformation of the ovine complex is essentially identical to class 1 of the bovine respirasome.
source: The tight conformation of the ovine complex is essentially identical to class 1 of the bovine respirasome, but the arrangement of component complexes in the loose state differs considerably from our class 2.
evidence: This is a comparison with the published ovine structure.

claim: In the bovine respirasome, complex III rotates by 25° relative to complex I, while the position of complex IV remains unchanged.
source: In the bovine respirasome, complex III rotates by 25° relative to complex I, while the position of complex IV remains unchanged.
evidence: This describes the conformational change in the bovine structure.

claim: In the loose ovine respirasome, complex IV swings away from complex III.
source: In contrast, in the loose ovine respirasome, complex IV swings away from complex III.
evidence: This is a comparison with the published ovine structure.

claim: In both the bovine and the ovine respirasome, interactions between complex III and IV are disrupted in the minor classes.
source: In both the bovine and the ovine respirasome, interactions between complex III and IV are disrupted in these minor classes.
evidence: This is a comparison between the bovine and ovine structures.

claim: The proportion of particles in the loose state of the ovine respirasome was found to increase with time.
source: In the case of the ovine complex, the proportion of particles in the loose state was found to increase with time (Letts et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is cited from the ovine respirasome study.

claim: The loose state of the ovine respirasome and class 2 of the bovine complex result from incipient denaturation during and after purification.
source: This suggests that the loose state of the ovine respirasome and our class 2 of the bovine complex result from incipient denaturation during and after purification.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison with the ovine study.

claim: The two iron-sulfur domains in the complex III dimer are both resolved in the porcine and ovine respirasome.
source: Surprisingly, the two iron-sulfur domains in the complex III dimer are both resolved in the porcine and ovine respirasome, whereas one of them is disordered in our structure of the bovine complex.
evidence: This is a comparison with the published structures.

claim: Neither the porcine nor ovine structure shows a mobile and therefore catalytically active Rieske protein.
source: Therefore neither of the two other structures shows a mobile and therefore catalytically active Rieske protein, as we observe in the bovine respirasome.
evidence: This is a comparison with the published structures.

claim: Letts et al propose that due to the close proximity between complex IV and the Rieske protein of the outer monomer of complex III, the iron-sulfur domain of the outer complex III monomer cannot undergo the conformational changes required for electron transfer.
source: Letts et al propose that due to the close proximity between complex IV and the Rieske protein of the outer monomer of complex III, the iron-sulfur domain of the outer complex III monomer cannot undergo the conformational changes required for electron transfer.
evidence: This is cited from the Letts et al study.

claim: Letts et al conclude that quinone oxidation is likely to take place in the central complex III monomer.
source: Letts et al conclude that quinone oxidation is likely to take place in the central complex III monomer.
evidence: This is cited from the Letts et al study.

claim: Neither the porcine nor ovine structure shows any direct protein-protein contacts that would inhibit domain movements of the Rieske protein.
source: This is consistent with our findings, although neither structure shows any direct protein-protein contacts that would inhibit domain movements.
evidence: This is a comparison with the published structures.

claim: Letts et al propose that quinone reduction in complex III should be catalyzed by the distal monomer.
source: Letts et al also propose that quinone reduction in complex III should be catalyzed by the distal monomer; however the respirasome structures provide no evidence for this.
evidence: This is cited from the Letts et al study with a critical comment.

claim: The mitochondrial respirasome has a clear role for the long-term stability of its component complexes, in particular complex I.
source: Far from being a random collection of close-packed respiratory chain complexes, the mitochondrial respirasome has not only a clear role for the long-term stability of its component complexes, in particular complex I, but also in optimizing electron flow in cellular respiration.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural and functional analysis.

claim: The mitochondrial respirasome has a role in optimizing electron flow in cellular respiration.
source: Far from being a random collection of close-packed respiratory chain complexes, the mitochondrial respirasome has not only a clear role for the long-term stability of its component complexes, in particular complex I, but also in optimizing electron flow in cellular respiration.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the structural and functional analysis.

claim: Bovine heart mitochondria were prepared by differential centrifugation.
source: Bovine heart mitochondria were prepared by differential centrifugation as described (Krause et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a methodological statement with a citation.

claim: Mitochondria were solubilized with 1% (w/v) digitonin at a detergent-to-protein ratio of 28:1.
source: Mitochondria were solubilized with 1% (w/v) digitonin (Calbiochem) at a detergent-to-protein ratio of 28:1 (Schäfer et al., 2006) or with 0.11% (w/v) PCC-a-M (Glycon) at a detergent-to-protein ratio of 1:1 by incubation for 1 hr at 4°C.
evidence: This is a methodological statement with a citation.

claim: Mitochondria were solubilized with 0.11% (w/v) PCC-a-M at a detergent-to-protein ratio of 1:1.
source: Mitochondria were solubilized with 1% (w/v) digitonin (Calbiochem) at a detergent-to-protein ratio of 28:1 (Schäfer et al., 2006) or with 0.11% (w/v) PCC-a-M (Glycon) at a detergent-to-protein ratio of 1:1 by incubation for 1 hr at 4°C.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.

claim: Detergent exchange to amphipol A8-35 and protein purification were performed as described before.
source: Detergent exchange to amphipol A8-35 and protein purification were performed as described before (Althoff et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological statement with a citation.

claim: Cryo-EM images were collected on a FEI Tecnai Polara operating at 300 kV.
source: Cryo-EM images were collected on a FEI Tecnai Polara operating at 300 kV aligned as previously described (Mills et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological statement with a citation.

claim: The microscope was equipped with a Falcon III direct electron detector.
source: The microscope was equipped with a Falcon III direct electron detector.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.

claim: Images were recorded at a nominal magnification of 59,000x yielding a pixel size at the specimen of 1.77 Å.
source: Images were recorded manually at a nominal magnification of 59,000x yielding a pixel size at the specimen of 1.77 Å.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.

claim: Videos were collected for 1.5 s with a total of 46 frames with a calibrated dose of about 1.5 e-/Å2 per frame.
source: Videos were collected for 1.5 s with a total of 46 frames with a calibrated dose of about 1.5 e-/Å2 per frame, at defocus values between −1.3 and −4.3 μm.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.

claim: A set of 3592 micrographs was collected.
source: A set of 3592 micrographs was collected.
evidence: This is a methodological statement.

claim: The cryo-EM maps were deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank with accession code EMD-4107, EMD-4108 and EM-4109.
source: The cryo-EM maps were deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank with accession code EMD-4107, EMD-4108 and EM-4109 for the cryo-EM maps of class 1, 2 and 3, respectively and the structure coordinates of the complexes fitted to class 1 were deposited in the Protein Data Bank with accession number 5LUF.
evidence: This is a data deposition statement.

claim: The structure coordinates of the complexes fitted to class 1 were deposited in the Protein Data Bank with accession number 5LUF.
source: The cryo-EM maps were deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank with accession code EMD-4107, EMD-4108 and EM-4109 for the cryo-EM maps of class 1, 2 and 3, respectively and the structure coordinates of the complexes fitted to class 1 were deposited in the Protein Data Bank with accession number 5LUF.
evidence: This is a data deposition statement.
